title: URL Shortener
blurb: Read-heavy service: ID generation, caching, redirects, analytics

explanation.summary: Turns a long URL into a short code and redirects anyone who opens the code. It is a classic read-heavy system: one link is created once and opened many times, so the design is mostly about fast lookups.

title: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
blurb: Authentication vs authorization, roles, permissions, JWT claims

explanation.summary: Instead of granting permissions to each user, you grant them to roles (admin, editor, viewer) and give users roles. Access checks become "does any of this user's roles include this permission?".

title: Uber Surge Pricing & Artificial Scarcity
blurb: Supply and demand per hexagon, gamed logouts, and how to price robustly

explanation.summary: Surge pricing raises the price where riders outnumber free drivers, to pull more drivers in. Because the price reacts to supply, drivers can fake a shortage by going offline together: artificial scarcity. A robust design prices from smoothed, sanity-checked supply and locks the price the rider sees.

title: Docker vs Virtual Machines
blurb: Virtual machines vs containers: what each one shares, images and layers, and when to use which

explanation.summary: A virtual machine (VM) is a whole computer made in software: it boots its own operating system. A container is just a walled-off program that shares the host's kernel, the core of the operating system. VMs have stronger walls; containers are much lighter and start in about a second.

title: Twitter Timeline & Search
blurb: Fan-out on write, celebrity merge at read time, caching and search
chapters: Step 4: Write API → Fan Out Service
Step 6: Fan Out Service → Search Cluster
Step 7: Fan Out Service → Notification Service

explanation.summary: Users post tweets, read a home timeline built from everyone they follow, and search. Reads dwarf writes, so the home timeline is precomputed: each new tweet is pushed into followers' timelines in memory (fan-out on write), except for celebrities, whose tweets are merged in when a timeline is read.

title: Web Crawler & Search
blurb: Priority frontier, duplicate detection, reverse index, freshness

explanation.summary: A crawler keeps a priority queue of links, fetches the most important page, skips it if a near-identical page was already crawled, and otherwise queues it for indexing. Search reads only the reverse index (word → pages) and the stored titles and snippets.

title: Kafka: Event Streaming
blurb: Topics, partitions, consumer groups, copies across brokers, and what "delivered" really means

explanation.summary: Kafka is a log of events, spread across several servers and kept safely on disk. Producers add events to topics, which are split into partitions spread over brokers. Consumers read at their own pace and remember their place with offsets. Services no longer have to call each other directly, traffic spikes wait in the log, and many systems can react to the same event.

title: Idempotent Payments
blurb: "Payment failed" but money debited: lost responses, retries and idempotency keys

explanation.summary: A payment can succeed at the bank while its response is lost on the way back, so the app cannot tell success from failure. If it retries as a new request, the customer pays twice. The fix: the app sends an idempotency key, the server remembers the first result for that key and replays it, and a timeout is treated as "pending" and settled later by webhooks and reconciliation.

title: Mint: Personal Finance Aggregator
blurb: Pulling bank transactions through a queue, then categorizing and budgeting them

explanation.summary: Mint connects to a user's bank accounts, pulls their transactions, sorts each one into a category, and warns them when a monthly budget is close to its limit. The hard part is the pipeline: many slow, unreliable bank connections feeding a steady flow of writes. An extraction service, a queue, and small services for categories and budgets keep the user-facing side fast.

title: Pastebin
blurb: Short keys, metadata in SQL, text in an object store, expiry and caching

explanation.summary: A user pastes text and gets a short link; anyone with the link can read it until it expires. The text sits in an object store, a small row in SQL records the key and expiry, a cache serves hot pastes, and a background job removes expired ones.

title: Key-Value Store (Dynamo-style)
blurb: Hash ring, replication, quorum reads and writes, hinted handoff and LSM storage

explanation.summary: A key-value store only offers get(key) and put(key, value), which lets it spread over many machines and keep working when some fail. Keys are placed on a hash ring, each key is copied to N nodes, and quorum rules (W acks to write, R replies to read) let you choose between speed and fresh reads.

title: Social Network Graph
blurb: Friend lists across Person Servers, a lookup service, and shortest-path search

explanation.summary: A social network is a graph of people and friendships. The key feature is finding the shortest path between two people. The friend lists are too big for one machine, so they are split across Person Servers, a Lookup Service says which server holds whom, and a breadth-first search walks the graph in batches.

title: Amazon's Sales Rank by Category
blurb: Batch MapReduce over transaction logs, a ranked table, and a cache in front

explanation.summary: Each category shows its bestsellers for the past week. Purchases are appended to log files, a batch MapReduce job adds them up per category and product on a schedule, and the sorted result is stored in an analytics table and cached. Shoppers read the finished table, so reading is fast and the order path is untouched.

title: Query Cache for a Search Engine
blurb: LRU caching, sharded memory, TTLs and invalidation for hot searches

explanation.summary: A search engine answers the same popular queries again and again. Computing each answer means reading posting lists and fetching documents, which is slow. So the Query API keeps the results of recent queries in a sharded in-memory cache with LRU eviction, and only searches the index on a miss.

title: Scaling to Millions of Users on AWS
blurb: From one server to millions of users: load balancing, caching, queues and shards, one bottleneck at a time

explanation.summary: No system starts with millions of users. This topic follows one app from a single server to a big fleet, adding one idea at each stage: give the database its own machine, balance and cache, scale automatically and move slow work to a queue, then split the database. Add each piece only when a number you measure runs out.

title: Rate Limiter
blurb: Token bucket, fixed and sliding windows, and what to do when the counter store is down

reels.title: Fixed window
reels.blurb: One counter per minute: the cheapest limit, and why it can let 20 through in 10 seconds

reels.title: Sliding window log
reels.blurb: Keep the time of every request: exact, and how much memory that costs

reels.title: Sliding window counter
reels.blurb: Two counters and a weighted sum: 10 × 0.917 + 0 = 9.17, worked through

reels.title: Token bucket
reels.blurb: 10 tokens, one back every 6 seconds: bursts allowed, the average held

explanation.summary: A rate limiter caps how many requests a caller can make in a period. It protects services from abuse and overload, keeps one noisy client from starving the rest, and enforces paid plans. The hard parts are choosing the counting algorithm, counting correctly across many servers, and deciding what happens when the counter store is down.

title: Retries: Backoff and Jitter
blurb: Why retrying at once makes an outage worse: exponential backoff, jitter, retry budgets and dead letters

explanation.summary: When a call fails, trying again often works: the server was busy for a moment, or a packet was lost. But if every client retries at once, and keeps retrying, the extra traffic keeps the server down. Exponential backoff waits longer after each failure; jitter makes each client wait a random part of that time; limits and budgets stop retries from multiplying.

title: API Gateway
blurb: One front door for many services: tokens, rate limits, routing, caching and circuit breakers

explanation.summary: An API gateway is the one front door for all the services behind it. It checks who is calling, limits how often, picks the right service, can cache answers, and stops calling a service that is failing. Services then focus on business logic. The hard parts are keeping the gateway fast and thin, and deciding what to do when a service behind it breaks.

title: Consistent Hashing
blurb: How a cache or database cluster adds and loses nodes without reshuffling every key

explanation.summary: Consistent hashing is a way to spread keys over a changing set of servers so that adding or removing a server moves only a small share of the keys. Servers and keys are hashed onto the same ring; a key belongs to the first server clockwise from it. It is used by caches, sharded databases, CDNs and load balancers.

title: Chat System (WhatsApp-style)
blurb: WebSockets, store-then-deliver, groups, presence and offline push

explanation.summary: Users keep a WebSocket open to a gateway. A sent message is stored first, then delivered through a queue to the gateway holding the recipient's connection. Offline users get a push notification and catch up from their last message id when they return.

title: Scaling WebSockets vs HTTP
blurb: Why a server that keeps connections open scales differently: connections not requests, pub/sub between servers, heartbeats, reconnect storms, and Socket.IO vs plain WebSockets

explanation.summary: An HTTP server answers short, independent requests, so a load balancer can send each one anywhere and you scale by adding servers. A WebSocket server holds long-lived connections: each one stays on the server it reached, carries state, and can be pushed to at any time. That changes everything about scaling: you size by connections, every server must hear broadcasts through pub/sub, quiet connections need heartbeats, and restarts cause reconnect storms.

title: CDN: Content Delivery Network
blurb: Caches close to your visitors: cache keys, how long to keep files, a shield for your server, purging and hit ratio

explanation.summary: A CDN (content delivery network) is a worldwide network of caches placed close to visitors. The first request for a file travels to your own server, called the origin; the CDN keeps a copy, so later requests are answered from a few kilometres away. Pages load faster, your server does less work, and traffic spikes and attacks hit the CDN instead.

title: Notification System
blurb: Push, email and SMS at scale: dedup, preferences, queues, retries and dead letters

explanation.summary: A notification system turns events ("your order shipped") into messages on the right channel (push, email, SMS) without annoying people or losing important ones. The core design is: accept events fast, check preferences, put messages on per-channel queues, and let workers deliver them with retries.

title: Unique ID Generator (Snowflake)
blurb: Time-sorted 64-bit ids from many machines, with no coordination and no duplicates

explanation.summary: Every row needs an id that nobody else will ever use, even when many servers create rows at the same time. A Snowflake-style generator packs the time, the machine and a counter into one 64-bit number, so each machine can make ids alone, with no database and no talking to the others.

title: Ticket Booking System (BookMyShow-style)
blurb: Sell 18k seats to 600k fans in minutes: waiting room, timed seat holds and no double booking

explanation.summary: Selling tickets looks like a shop, but for a popular show many thousands of fans want the same few seats at the same second. A good design lets fans in at a safe speed, holds a seat for a short time while they pay, and makes it impossible to sell one seat twice.

title: Distributed Job Scheduler (Cron at Scale)
blurb: Run millions of jobs on time: a due-time poller, leased runs, retries with backoff and no double runs

explanation.summary: Cron runs a command at a set time on one machine. A distributed scheduler does the same for millions of jobs on many machines, and must still run each job once at its time, survive crashed workers and retry failures without hiding them.

title: Search Autocomplete (Typeahead)
blurb: Prefix trie with precomputed top-k, layered caches, and a pipeline that learns from searches

explanation.summary: Autocomplete shows likely searches as the user types. Each keystroke is a prefix lookup that must come back in roughly 100 ms, for billions of searches. The design has two halves: a fast serving path (caches in front of an in-memory trie that already knows the top suggestions for every prefix) and a slow learning path that turns the query log into a fresh trie.

title: Proximity Service (Nearby Places)
blurb: Find places within a radius of you in milliseconds, using geohash cells instead of scanning every row

explanation.summary: Apps like Yelp and Google Maps must answer "what is near me?" in milliseconds out of hundreds of millions of places. The trick is to cut the map into labelled cells (geohashes) and keep a list of places per cell, so a search reads a few small lists instead of scanning every row.

title: Video Streaming (YouTube-style)
blurb: Chunked upload, transcoding into a bitrate ladder, adaptive streaming and CDN delivery

explanation.summary: A video platform has two jobs. The upload path accepts a huge file, converts it into many sizes and splits each into short segments. The playback path hands every viewer the right size, a few seconds at a time, from a cache close to them. Storage is cheap; delivering the bytes is the expensive part.

title: Metrics & Monitoring System
blurb: Collecting millions of samples a second, storing them as compressed time series, and alerting without false pages

explanation.summary: A monitoring system collects numbers from every server (CPU, requests, errors, latency), stores them as time series, draws them on dashboards and wakes someone when something is wrong. The write load is huge and steady, reads are mostly recent data, and the alerting path must keep working exactly when everything else is on fire.

title: Circuit Breaker and Resilience Patterns
blurb: Timeouts, retries with backoff, circuit breakers and bulkheads: keeping one slow service from taking everything down

explanation.summary: When a service you call gets slow, your threads pile up waiting for it, and soon your whole app is down too. A few small patterns stop that: timeouts bound the wait, retries with backoff ride out short glitches, a circuit breaker stops calling a service that is failing, and a bulkhead keeps its trouble in one corner of your app.

title: File Sync (Dropbox-style)
blurb: Block-level sync: chunk and hash files, upload only what changed, and tell other devices

explanation.summary: A sync service keeps the same folder identical on all of a person's devices. The trick is to never treat a file as one lump: cut it into blocks, name each block by a hash of its bytes, and send only the blocks the server does not already have. A small metadata record says which blocks make up each version of each file.

title: Collaborative Editing (Google Docs-style)
blurb: Many people typing in one document: operational transformation, a server that orders edits, and snapshots

explanation.summary: In a shared document, two people can type at the same moment. Each edit says "put this at position 4", but if someone else's edit lands first, position 4 is no longer the right place. Operational transformation rewrites each edit against the edits before it, and one server puts all edits of a document in a single order, so every screen ends with the same text.

title: Leader Election (Raft)
blurb: How a cluster agrees on one leader: terms, votes, heartbeats and fencing

explanation.summary: Many systems need exactly one node in charge: the primary of a database, the owner of a shard, the holder of a lock. Leader election lets a group of nodes agree on that one node, and agree again quickly when it fails. Raft does it with terms, votes from a majority, and heartbeats.

title: Distributed Message Queue
blurb: Visibility timeouts, acks, retries and dead-letter queues, and why delivery is at least once

explanation.summary: A message queue sits between a producer that has work and the workers that do it. The producer drops a message and moves on; workers take messages at their own pace. The interesting part is failure: a worker that crashes must not lose the message, and one bad message must not block the rest. Queues solve this with acknowledgements, a visibility timeout, retries and a dead-letter queue, and the price is that a message can be delivered more than once.

title: Types of Queues
blurb: Standard, FIFO, priority, delay, pub/sub, request/reply, in-memory and bounded queues: what each promises

explanation.summary: A queue holds messages until a worker takes them, but queues make different promises. A standard queue is fast and keeps order only roughly. A FIFO queue keeps order within a group. A priority queue serves urgent work first. A delay queue hides a message until later. Pub/sub copies one message to many queues, request/reply sends an answer back, an in-memory queue trades safety for speed, and a bounded queue decides what happens when it is full.

title: Locking: Redis & Database
blurb: Shared, exclusive, update and intent locks, Redis locks with fencing, and when to use which

explanation.summary: When two requests read the same thing and then change it, both can act on a value that is already out of date. A lock makes them take turns. Databases lock rows and tables for you; Redis can lock anything by name across many servers, but only for a limited time.

title: Distributed Cache
blurb: Cache-aside on a sharded Redis cluster: hash slots, eviction policies and cache stampedes

explanation.summary: A distributed cache keeps hot data in the memory of several servers, so most reads never touch the database. The hard parts are splitting keys across servers, choosing what to throw out when memory is full, keeping the cache from going stale, and not letting a burst of misses crush the database.

title: Database Sharding
blurb: How to split one table over many databases, and why the choice of shard key decides everything

explanation.summary: Sharding splits one large table into pieces (shards) and puts each piece on its own database server. A shard key decides which shard owns a row, and a router sends each query to the right shard. It lets storage and write traffic grow beyond one machine, at the price of harder queries, joins and transactions.

title: RAG Pipeline
blurb: Answering from your own documents: chunking, embeddings, hybrid search, reranking and citations

explanation.summary: A language model only knows its training data. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) finds the passages of your own documents that answer a question, puts them in the prompt, and asks the model to answer only from them, with citations.

title: Vector Database
blurb: Finding the nearest of 100 million embeddings in milliseconds: flat scans, HNSW, IVF-PQ, recall and filters

explanation.summary: An embedding model turns a photo or a sentence into a list of numbers that captures what it means. A vector database stores millions of these and finds the ones nearest to a query in milliseconds, by searching an approximate index instead of comparing with every vector.

title: LLM Gateway
blurb: One front door for every model: keys and budgets, routing, token limits, fallbacks, caching and guardrails

explanation.summary: An LLM gateway sits between a company's apps and the model providers they call. It holds the real API keys, gives each team its own virtual key and budget, routes each request to a suitable model, caches safe answers, keeps calls under the providers' token limits, fails over when a provider is down, masks personal data and logs the cost of every call.

title: AI Agent with Tools
blurb: A language model in a loop that calls tools: step limits, tool policy, prompt injection and idempotent actions

explanation.summary: An AI agent is a language model in a loop that can call tools: functions such as searching, booking or sending email. The model decides the next step; a runtime around it runs the tools, feeds the results back, and enforces what the model may do, how long it may run and which actions need a person.

title: Model Weights & LLM Inference
blurb: What model weights are, how much GPU memory a model needs, quantization, the KV cache and serving your own model with vLLM

explanation.summary: A large language model is a file of numbers called weights, learned in training. Running it, called inference, means loading those weights into GPU memory and passing your tokens through them. The weights' size decides which GPU you need; whatever memory is left holds the KV cache, which decides how many conversations run at once; and because every new token reads all the weights, memory speed decides how fast answers come.

title: LLM Guardrails: Hallucinations & Evals
blurb: Stop an assistant making things up: grounding, citation checks, a judge model, handing over to a human, and the evals that prove it works

explanation.summary: A language model can write a confident answer that is simply wrong: a hallucination. Guardrails are the checks around the model that stop those answers reaching people. Ground the answer in your own documents, check its citations with code, let a judge model score what code can't check, and hand over to a human when a check fails. Evals, a fixed set of questions with known right answers, measure how well all of it works and block changes that make it worse.

title: Context Engineering for Long-Running Agents
blurb: Keep an agent working for hours inside a fixed context window: compaction, notes, clearing tool results, sub-agents, and the harness that runs it all

explanation.summary: An agent is a language model in a loop: it calls a tool, reads the result, and decides the next step. The model remembers nothing between calls, so every step resends the whole conversation, and the context grows until it fills the window. Context engineering is choosing what the model sees at each step: clearing old tool results, compacting the history into a summary, keeping notes outside the context, and handing exploration to sub-agents.

title: LangChain: Building LLM Apps
blurb: Standard pieces for LLM apps: one interface for every model, tools, retrievers, and an agent loop with middleware

explanation.summary: LangChain is an open-source library (for JavaScript and Python) of standard pieces for apps built on large language models: one interface for every model provider, messages, tools, retrievers and structured output. Its createAgent function runs the usual agent loop: the model asks for tools, LangChain runs them and feeds back the results, until the model answers. Middleware adds approvals, limits and clean-up around each step, and a checkpointer saves each conversation.

title: LangGraph: Stateful Agent Workflows
blurb: An LLM workflow as a graph: shared state, nodes, branching edges, checkpoints, pauses for a person and time travel

explanation.summary: LangGraph is an open-source library (JavaScript and Python) for building LLM workflows and agents as graphs. Nodes are functions, edges choose what runs next, and every node reads and updates one shared state. A checkpointer saves that state after every step under a thread_id, so a run can pause for a person, survive a restart, resume later and be replayed. LangChain's createAgent runs on it.

title: AWS VPC Networking
blurb: Your own network in AWS: address ranges, public and private subnets, route tables, NAT gateways and endpoints

explanation.summary: A VPC (virtual private cloud) is your own private network in one AWS region, with a range of addresses you choose. You split it into subnets in several Availability Zones. Each subnet's route table decides where its traffic can go: to the internet, through a NAT gateway, straight to an AWS service, or only inside the VPC.

title: Application Load Balancer
blurb: One HTTPS address for many services: listeners, rules, target groups, health checks and how a target is picked

explanation.summary: An Application Load Balancer (ALB) is AWS's load balancer for web traffic. Listeners accept connections on a port and decrypt HTTPS. Rules look at each request's host, path or headers and send it to a target group. Health checks keep broken targets from getting requests.

title: Global vs Local Load Balancing
blurb: Route 53, Global Accelerator, API Gateway and ALB: which layer picks the region, which checks the request, which picks the server, and how fast each fails over

explanation.summary: An app that runs in two regions needs three kinds of routing. A global load balancer (Route 53 with DNS, or Global Accelerator with anycast IP addresses) sends each user to a healthy region near them. An API gateway checks each request (tokens, rate limits) and routes it to the right service. A local load balancer (an ALB) spreads requests across healthy servers in the region's zones. Each layer handles a different failure, at a different speed.

title: ECS on Fargate
blurb: Running containers with no servers to manage: task definitions, services, scaling on CPU and safe deploys

explanation.summary: Amazon ECS (Elastic Container Service) runs copies of your container, called tasks. A service keeps the number you ask for running and adds them to a load balancer. On Fargate, AWS gives each task its own small virtual machine, so there are no servers for you to look after. You choose CPU and memory for each task and pay for them by the second.

title: Full-stack App on ECS
blurb: A Vue client and a Node API on ECS, with DynamoDB and S3, shipped by a pipeline with blue/green deploys

explanation.summary: A complete AWS setup for a web app. A Vue.js client and a Node.js API run as two ECS services, each behind its own load balancer, with DynamoDB and S3 for data. A pipeline (CodePipeline) builds every commit with CodeBuild and ships it with CodeDeploy blue/green deploys. Everything is described in Terraform.

title: Load Balancer
blurb: Sharing requests across servers: how it picks one, health checks, and what happens when something fails

explanation.summary: A load balancer sits in front of a group of identical servers and hands each request to one of them. You can add servers when traffic grows, broken servers stop getting requests, and users only ever see one address.

title: Redis Basics: Data Types
blurb: Strings, hashes, lists, sets and sorted sets, with TTLs and atomic commands, by real use case

explanation.summary: Redis is an in-memory data store. Instead of plain values, it stores data types (strings, hashes, lists, sets and sorted sets) with commands that change them in place, and it runs one command at a time, so each command is atomic. Keys can expire on their own.

title: Redis Persistence and Replication
blurb: RDB snapshots, the AOF, replicas, Sentinel failover and split brain: what each failure really loses

explanation.summary: Redis keeps data in memory, so what survives a failure depends on two separate choices: persistence (RDB snapshots and the append-only file) decides what a restarted node still has, and replication with Sentinel decides whether another node takes over, and how fast. Replication is asynchronous, so failovers and network splits can lose acknowledged writes.

title: Redis Replication, Sentinel and Cluster
blurb: How replicas sync, how Sentinel fails over, and how Redis Cluster shards keys into 16,384 slots

explanation.summary: Replication keeps copies of a Redis primary on other machines. Sentinel watches a primary and promotes a replica when it dies. Redis Cluster splits the keys into 16,384 slots across several primaries, each with its own replicas, and fails each shard over by itself. All three copy data asynchronously, so a failover can lose the last few writes.

title: AWS Basics: What the Cloud Is and Why
blurb: Buying servers or renting them, regions and Availability Zones, Auto Scaling and Lambda, and what each one costs

explanation.summary: AWS (Amazon Web Services) rents out computing: servers, storage, databases and networks, by the hour or by the request. Instead of buying hardware for your busiest hour and waiting weeks for more, you start what you need in minutes, spread it across data centres, and pay for what you use. The catch is a bill you have to plan for and watch.

title: AWS IAM: Who Can Do What
blurb: Who can do what in AWS: users, roles and JSON policies, and how AWS decides yes or no

explanation.summary: IAM (Identity and Access Management) decides whether each request to AWS is allowed. Every request is signed by an identity: a user, or a role with short-lived credentials. AWS gathers every policy that applies and checks them. One explicit Deny anywhere means no, and if nothing says Allow, the answer is also no.

title: Disaster Recovery Across AWS Regions
blurb: How fast you must come back and how much data you may lose (RTO and RPO), AWS's four strategies, and why a copy is not a backup

explanation.summary: Disaster recovery (DR) is how a system comes back after losing a whole region, or its data. Two targets shape the design: RTO, how long it may be down, and RPO, how much recent data it may lose. AWS describes four strategies, from backup and restore (cheap, hours) to active/active in two regions (costly, almost instant). None of them replaces point-in-time backups.

title: Kafka Basics: Topics, Partitions, Groups
blurb: Events in a log you only add to: keys pick partitions, consumer groups share them, and offsets let anyone read again

explanation.summary: Kafka stores events in topics. A topic is a log you only add to, split into partitions. The hash of each event's key picks its partition, which keeps each key's events in order. Consumers in a group share the partitions, one consumer per partition, and save their place as offsets. So many groups can read the same events, and any of them can go back and read again.

title: Kafka Reliability: Durability, Exactly-Once
blurb: In-sync copies, acks and min.insync.replicas, unclean leader election, idempotent producers, transactions and rebalances

explanation.summary: Kafka's promises come from its settings. Copies with acks=all and min.insync.replicas decide which confirmed messages survive a broker failing. Unclean leader election chooses between staying up and keeping data. Idempotent producers remove the repeats that retries cause. Transactions make "read, process, write" happen exactly once inside Kafka.

title: Terraform Basics: Plan, Apply, State
blurb: Infrastructure as code: resources, the order Terraform works in, updating vs replacing, drift, and why the state file matters

explanation.summary: Terraform turns .tf files that describe the infrastructure you want into the API calls that build it. It keeps a state file that links each resource in your code to a real one. It checks that state against the real world, compares it with your code, and shows a plan: create, update in place, replace or destroy. Apply carries out the plan in the right order and saves the new state.

title: Terraform Remote State and Locking
blurb: Why state lives in S3, how a lock stops two applies at once, and what lost resources and stuck locks look like

explanation.summary: Terraform's state file is its memory of what it manages, so a team must share one copy and never write it twice at the same time. A remote backend such as S3 shares it, versioning keeps every earlier copy, and a lock makes a second run wait. When a run dies halfway, stuck locks and forgotten resources need careful cleaning up.

title: Terraform Modules and Environments
blurb: Copied folders vs workspaces vs versioned modules: limiting damage, moving changes from dev to prod, and guarding against deletes

explanation.summary: A Terraform module packs resources behind inputs and outputs, so one part can be reused in every environment. How you lay out your environments decides how much one change can break. Copied folders drift apart, and workspaces all run the same code version. Versioned modules, with a separate configuration and state for each environment, let you move a change forward step by step and keep mistakes small.

title: Ad Click Aggregator
blurb: Counting billions of ad clicks per minute: windows, late events, duplicates and exact billing

explanation.summary: An advertiser pays each time a viewer clicks an ad, so the count must be right and must show up fast. The design logs every click, counts them in one-minute windows on a stream, skips duplicates, and fixes the numbers every night from the raw log.
